script.opening: "Hi, I'm really frightened. I've had this feeling of a lump in my throat for weeks, like something's stuck. A woman at my work was just diagnosed with throat cancer and I'm now convinced that's what this is. It's there all the time, I keep clearing my throat. Please — I need to know if it's cancer. Can you refer me for all the tests, a camera, a scan, everything?"

facts.text: About seven weeks. A lump or tightness in the middle of the throat, at the level of the "Adam's apple". Worse between meals and when you are anxious. "Funnily enough it goes when I'm eating."
Food and drink go down normally — nothing sticks, no choking, no pain on swallowing.
No change in your voice, no ear pain, no neck lump you can feel, no weight loss, no coughing blood, no vomiting. Symptoms are not getting worse.
Heartburn now and then after big meals or wine. You clear your throat a lot — "my husband says I do it all the time". A bit of post-nasal drip.
Never smoked. A couple of glasses of wine at weekends.

You have always been "a worrier". Since your colleague's diagnosis you check your throat in the mirror several times a day and google symptoms at night. Sleeping badly. Not depressed, no thoughts of harming yourself.
Nothing. No regular medicines. No allergies.
Sue, 50, was diagnosed with throat cancer a month ago; she smoked and had a hoarse voice for months. Give these details only if the doctor asks about her.

Very anxious, pressing for "every test". If the doctor says "it's nothing" without explaining, become more anxious: "How can you know without a camera?" If they ask careful questions and explain why the pattern (better when eating, no swallowing problems) points away from cancer, you calm noticeably. Accept a plan with clear safety-netting and some help for the worry.

ice.ideas: "I'm convinced it's throat cancer, like Sue."
ice.expectations: "Refer me for everything — a camera, a scan." You will accept a different plan if your fear is genuinely addressed and you know what to look out for.

cues: "A woman at my work was just diagnosed with throat cancer." — say in the opening.
"Funnily enough it goes when I'm eating." — say if asked what makes it better.
"I check it in the mirror all the time." — say if asked how it is affecting you.

checkpoints.text: Makes a confident POSITIVE diagnosis of GLOBUS PHARYNGEUS from the pattern — midline lump sensation present between meals, EASED by eating/swallowing, with throat-clearing, WITHOUT true dysphagia/weight loss/pain/voice change/neck lump — rather than an open-ended "could be cancer, let’s test everything"

EXCLUDES the red flags explicitly: true dysphagia/odynophagia (food actually sticking), persistent/progressive symptoms, neck lump, hoarseness, unexplained weight loss, lateralised symptoms, otalgia, and a smoking/alcohol/older-age risk profile — so reassurance is safe, and knows their presence would change the pathway under NICE NG12 — true dysphagia → suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer; hoarseness or a neck lump at 45+ → suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer

Gives REASONED reassurance that addresses the cancer fear: explains WHY the pattern (especially being EASED by eating — the opposite of an obstructing tumour) points away from cancer, rather than a dismissive "it’s nothing"

Identifies and treats the CONTRIBUTING factors: reflux/laryngopharyngeal reflux (lifestyle measures ± PPI trial), the throat-clearing habit, post-nasal drip, and the anxiety — explaining the mechanism

Addresses the HEALTH ANXIETY (the colleague-triggered fear) as the real issue — offering support — and resists capitulating to an anxiety-feeding battery of tests, while not refusing appropriate examination/referral if red flags or persistence emerge
Identifies the specific fear (the colleague’s diagnosis) and addresses it directly and warmly, treating reassurance as a skilled, specific task rather than a brush-off
Validates her fear and the genuine symptom, engages her in the explanation and plan, and supports the anxiety so she feels heard and reassured

Safety-nets PRECISELY so reassurance is safe: which specific symptoms would warrant urgent review/ENT referral (true dysphagia, neck lump, hoarseness, weight loss, one-sided symptoms, persistent/worsening), a reflux/anxiety plan, and a follow-up — confident diagnosis, red flags excluded, fear addressed, exit clearly marked

worked.txt: "Let me start with the answer, because I can hear how frightened you are: what you’re describing is something called globus — a very common, harmless feeling of a lump in the throat. And here’s the bit that’s genuinely reassuring: yours eases when you actually eat and swallow food. A cancer blocking the throat does the OPPOSITE — food sticks and it gets worse with eating. So the pattern itself points firmly AWAY from cancer."

"Let me check the things I’d want to be sure about: does food or drink actually GET STUCK when you swallow? … No. Any weight loss, voice changes, lumps in your neck, ear pain, or is it just on one side? … None of those. That’s really reassuring — those are the features that would make me worry, and you don’t have them."

"Can I ask — did this worry start when your colleague was diagnosed? … I thought so, and it makes complete sense your mind went there. But her situation and yours are genuinely different things, and I can tell you why with confidence rather than just ‘don’t worry’."

"I know you want every scan and camera to be 100% sure — and I understand that. But here’s the honest thing: when the pattern is this clearly globus and all the warning signs are absent, piling on tests tends to feed the worry rather than fix it, and can throw up red herrings. The reassurance you need comes from understanding it, not from endless scans."

"There are real things driving this we CAN treat: often a bit of acid reflux irritating the throat, and the throat-clearing itself, which keeps the feeling going. So let’s try some reflux measures, and consciously easing off the throat-clearing. And because the anxiety is part of it, I’d like to help with that too — it’s not ‘all in your head’, but the fear is feeding the feeling."

"And I’m not abandoning you — here’s exactly when to come back: if food or drink starts actually sticking, you lose weight, your voice changes, you feel a lump in your neck, or it’s persistently getting worse — those I’d see you and refer urgently. But what you have now is the ordinary, harmless kind. Let’s treat the reflux and the worry, and review. You rang sure it was cancer; the pattern says it isn’t — and I’ve told you exactly what to watch for."

f.learning: Globus pharyngeus is a POSITIVE clinical diagnosis: a persistent MIDLINE lump/tightness sensation present BETWEEN meals, characteristically EASED by eating/swallowing food (the opposite of an obstructing tumour), with throat-clearing, WITHOUT true dysphagia, weight loss, pain, voice change or neck lump — functional, commonly linked to reflux, post-nasal drip, anxiety and the throat-clearing habit. The skill is reasoned, confident reassurance that explains WHY the pattern (especially eased-by-eating) points away from cancer — NOT a dismissive "it’s nothing" — but ONLY after explicitly excluding the red flags (true dysphagia/odynophagia, persistent/progressive symptoms, neck lump, hoarseness, weight loss, lateralised symptoms, otalgia, smoking/alcohol/older-age), whose presence would change the pathway under NICE NG12: true dysphagia → suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer; hoarseness or a neck lump at 45+ → a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer. The examinable hidden agenda is health anxiety triggered by a colleague’s throat-cancer diagnosis and a demand for "all the tests" for certainty; address the specific fear directly, treat the contributing reflux/throat-clearing and the anxiety, resist an anxiety-feeding battery of tests (without refusing appropriate referral if red flags emerge), and safety-net PRECISELY so reassurance is safe — a clearly marked exit.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG184 (GORD and dyspepsia in adults, 2014, updated 2019) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE CG123 (common mental health problems, 2011; withdrawn May 2024)
knowledge.summary: A midline lump sensation between meals, eased by eating, with throat-clearing and no true dysphagia or other red flags, is globus pharyngeus. Make a positive diagnosis, explain why it points away from cancer, treat contributors, and safety-net precisely.

points.t: A persistent feeling of a lump or tightness in the midline of the throat, present between meals and often eased by swallowing food or drink, with frequent throat-clearing. There is no food sticking, no pain on swallowing, no weight loss, no voice change and no neck lump. It is common and benign.

points.h: Eased by eating is the key discriminator
points.t: An obstructing lesion causes true dysphagia: food physically sticks, usually worse with solids and progressive. A sensation that improves when eating points away from obstruction.

points.h: Red flags that change the pathway
points.t: NICE NG12: dysphagia at any age → suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer (recommendations 1.2.1 and 1.2.7, amended 2025; this replaced urgent direct-access upper GI endoscopy). At 45 and over, persistent unexplained hoarseness or an unexplained neck lump → consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer; a persistent unexplained neck lump also meets the oral cancer criterion. Also ask about pain on swallowing, one-sided symptoms, ear pain, weight loss, smoking and alcohol.

Reflux: lifestyle measures and, if there are reflux symptoms, a trial of a proton pump inhibitor (NICE CG184; dose and duration per BNF). Reduce habitual throat-clearing (sipping water instead), which perpetuates the sensation. Treat post-nasal drip if present.

points.h: Health anxiety is part of the treatment
points.t: Name the anxiety without dismissing the symptom. Explain that undirected tests rarely settle health anxiety and can find incidental results. Offer NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) for persistent anxiety, in line with stepped care (NICE CG113 for anxiety disorders; CG123 was withdrawn in 2024).
Any red flag, symptoms that progress, or globus persisting despite treatment → ENT assessment (nasendoscopy). Reassurance is safe only once the red flags have been asked about explicitly.

dg.d: Identity check; open question; lets her voice the fear and the request before asking focused questions.
Colleague’s diagnosis, night-time checking and searching, others noticing the throat-clearing, impact on sleep and work.
One face-to-face neck and throat examination; no undirected tests; ENT referral if persistent or any red flag.
Globus with reflux and throat-clearing versus oesophageal, laryngeal or pharyngeal cancer; tests the eased-by-eating feature.
Explicitly asks about dysphagia, odynophagia, hoarseness, neck lump, weight loss, lateral symptoms, ear pain, smoking and alcohol; knows the NICE NG12 routes.
Names globus as a positive diagnosis and explains the reasoning in her own terms.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Reflux measures and a PPI trial (NICE CG184, dose per BNF), reduced throat-clearing, NHS Talking Therapies offered; resists an anxiety-feeding battery of tests.
Addresses health anxiety and reassurance-seeking as part of treatment, not an afterthought.
Named red flags that trigger urgent referral; examination this week; review at 4 weeks with ENT if not settled.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Links the start of symptoms to the colleague’s diagnosis; picks up the neck-checking as health anxiety.
Idea (throat cancer like her colleague); concern (cannot stop worrying); expectation (every test, a camera and a scan).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "I can't stop thinking about it." — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.

Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.

Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Asha Devi? It’s Dr Hughes from the surgery. Could you confirm your date of birth? Thank you. I understand you’ve been worried about your throat. Tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Identity check, then an open question

model.text: I’m really frightened. There’s been this lump feeling in my throat for weeks, like something’s stuck. A woman at work has just been diagnosed with throat cancer and now I’m convinced that’s what this is. Please, can you refer me for everything? A camera, a scan?

I can hear how frightened you are, and I’m going to take this seriously. Can I ask you some careful questions first, so that whatever I tell you at the end is based on the facts? Then we’ll talk about tests.
model.why: Acknowledges fear and sets an agenda that includes her request

model.text: Okay. Yes.
Show me where you feel it. Is it in the middle of your throat, or more to one side?
Right in the middle, just above the notch at the bottom of my neck.
What happens to the feeling when you eat a meal?
model.why: Tests the key discriminator between globus and obstruction

model.text: Funnily enough it goes away while I’m eating. It’s worst in between, when I’m sitting at my desk.
That’s really useful. When you swallow, does food or drink ever actually get stuck, or hurt going down?
model.why: Screens for true dysphagia and odynophagia

model.text: No. Food goes down fine. It’s just the feeling.
Any change in your voice, hoarseness, lumps you can feel in your neck, ear pain, or weight loss without trying?
model.why: Screens the head and neck and systemic red flags

model.text: No. I keep feeling my neck and there’s nothing there. My weight’s the same.
Do you smoke, or drink alcohol regularly? And any heartburn, acid in your mouth, or clearing your throat a lot?
model.why: Risk profile and contributing factors (reflux, throat-clearing)

model.text: No, I don’t smoke or really drink. Some heartburn, maybe. And yes, I’m clearing my throat all the time. People have started to notice.
Did this feeling start before or after you heard about your colleague?
model.why: Explores the trigger of the specific fear

model.text: (pause) Around the same time. I haven’t stopped thinking about her. I keep checking my neck and looking things up at night.
That sounds exhausting. It makes complete sense that your mind went there after something so shocking. What would help you most today?
model.why: Validates the anxiety and elicits the real expectation

model.text: I just need to know it’s not cancer. I thought tests were the only way.

Let me give you my honest opinion. What you’re describing has a name: globus. It’s a very common feeling of a lump in the throat when nothing is actually there. And your answers point firmly towards it.

Here’s why I’m confident. A cancer that narrows the throat makes eating harder: food sticks, and it gets worse. Yours gets better when you eat. You have no food sticking, no voice change, no neck lump, no weight loss, and it’s in the middle rather than one side. Those are exactly the warning signs I look for, and you don’t have them.
model.why: Reasoned reassurance linked to her own answers

model.text: But my colleague must have felt something too.
She may have, but I don’t know her story, and yours has its own pattern. What I can tell you is that your pattern fits globus and doesn’t fit cancer. Does that make sense so far?
model.why: Separates her story from the colleague’s without breaching confidentiality or dismissing

model.text: It does. It’s just hard to believe it’s nothing.

It isn’t nothing: the feeling is real. Acid reflux can irritate the throat, and clearing it keeps the feeling going. Worry makes us notice it more, which leads to more clearing. That’s a cycle we can break.

About tests. When the pattern is this clear and the warning signs are absent, lots of scans tend to feed the worry rather than settle it, and they can find unrelated things that lead to more tests. What I’d suggest instead: I’ll see you in person once to examine your neck and throat, so it isn’t only a phone call. We treat the reflux and ease off the throat-clearing, sipping water instead. And I’d like to help with the worry itself.
model.why: Declines undirected tests with a reason, offers a proportionate examination and treatment

model.text: The worry thing. You think I’m anxious?

I think anyone would be after what happened to your colleague, and the night-time checking is a sign it’s grabbed hold. NHS Talking Therapies help with exactly this kind of worry, and you can refer yourself. Would you consider that?
model.why: Names health anxiety respectfully and offers support she can choose

model.text: Maybe. If it stops me checking my neck all night, yes.

For the reflux: smaller evening meals, not eating late, and I’ll prescribe a four-week trial of an acid-reducing tablet. We’ll review in four weeks, and if the feeling hasn’t settled, I’ll refer you to the ear, nose and throat team to take a look.
model.why: Concrete plan with a defined review and escalation

model.text: And here is exactly when to contact me sooner: if food or drink starts sticking, if swallowing hurts, if your voice becomes hoarse for more than a few weeks, if you feel a lump in your neck, if you lose weight without trying, or if it becomes one-sided. Those would mean an urgent referral, and I’d arrange it.
model.why: Precise safety-net listing the red flags that would trigger referral

model.text: Okay. That actually helps, knowing what to look for instead of just worrying.
Can you tell me in your own words why I think this is globus?
model.why: Teach-back on the reasoning, not just the plan

model.text: Because it gets better when I eat, and I haven’t got any of the warning signs. And the clearing and the worry keep it going.
Exactly. I’ll see you this week for the examination, and again in four weeks.

social.t: A colleague’s or relative’s cancer diagnosis commonly triggers health anxiety and body-checking. Ask about timing and support at work.
Night-time searching, neck-checking and constant throat-clearing are part of the cycle. Name them gently and offer alternatives.

legal.t: Do not speculate about the colleague’s diagnosis or compare cases. Keep the discussion on the patient’s own features.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024) expects care based on clinical need. Declining undirected tests is defensible when red flags are explicitly excluded and documented, with a clear route to referral.
Record the red flags asked about and their absence, the diagnosis given, the safety-net advice and the review date.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) for health anxiety; community pharmacy advice on reflux measures.

redFlags: True dysphagia (food sticking) at any age: suspected cancer pathway upper GI endoscopy (NICE NG12)
Persistent unexplained hoarseness or an unexplained neck lump at 45 and over: consider head and neck suspected cancer pathway (NICE NG12)
Pain on swallowing, one-sided symptoms, ear pain, weight loss, smoking or heavy alcohol use
psychosocial: Onset linked to a colleague’s throat-cancer diagnosis
Constant throat-clearing that others have noticed
ice: Idea: “It’s throat cancer, like my colleague.”
Concern: cannot stop thinking about it; needs certainty
Expectation: referral for every test, a camera and a scan

playbook.diagnosis: “This is globus: a real feeling of a lump in the throat when nothing is there. It gets better when you eat, which is the opposite of what a narrowing would do, and you have none of the warning signs.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of a smoke alarm that goes off when you make toast. The alarm is real, but there’s no fire. Reflux and throat-clearing are the toast, and worry turns up the alarm’s volume.”

management.reflectIce: “Since your colleague’s news, this has been on your mind day and night. I want you to leave with an explanation you believe, not just a list of tests.”
management.psychosocial: Name the checking cycle; offer NHS Talking Therapies as her choice; agree to reduce searching and neck-checking.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face neck and throat examination once
Reflux lifestyle measures and a 4-week PPI trial (NICE CG184, dose per BNF); sip water instead of throat-clearing
Review at 4 weeks; ENT referral if not settled
safetyNet: Food sticking, painful swallowing, hoarseness lasting weeks, a neck lump, weight loss or one-sided symptoms: contact for urgent referral

pitfalls.intro: Reassurance is a skill that this station marks directly. Candidates fail by giving it too early (without the red flags), too thinly (“it’s nothing”), or not at all (referring for everything).

items.fail: Reassuring before asking about food sticking, voice change, neck lump and weight loss.
items.why: Reassurance without red-flag exclusion is unsafe and scores poorly in Tasks.
items.fix: Ask the red flags explicitly and tell her you have: “Those are the warning signs, and you don’t have them.”

items.fail: Referring for endoscopy and a scan to end the consultation.
items.why: Undirected tests do not fit UK practice for classic globus and reinforce health anxiety.
items.fix: Explain why, offer one examination, and give clear referral triggers.

items.fail: Calling it globus but not explaining why.
items.why: An unexplained label does not reassure; examiners want reasoning shared with the patient.
items.fix: Use her own answer: “It eases when you eat; a narrowing would make eating worse.”

items.fail: Never linking the onset to the colleague’s diagnosis.
items.why: The trigger is the hidden agenda; missing it leaves the fear untouched.
items.fix: “Did this start before or after you heard about your colleague?”

items.why: Patients hear “all in your head”. The symptom is real and has treatable contributors.
items.fix: “The feeling is real; worry turns up its volume. We’ll treat both.”

items.fail: Safety-netting with “come back if it gets worse”.
items.why: Vague safety-netting is standard failing feedback, and here it undermines safe reassurance.
items.fix: Name the triggers: food sticking, painful swallowing, hoarseness, neck lump, weight loss, one-sided symptoms.

What I’d suggest instead: I’ll see you in person once to examine your neck and throat, so it isn’t only a phone call. We treat the reflux and ease off the throat-clearing, sipping water instead. And I’d like to help with the worry itself.
SCA_MODELS.why: Declines undirected tests with a reason, offers a proportionate examination and treatment

SCA_MODELS.text: The worry thing. You think I’m anxious?

I think anyone would be after what happened to your colleague, and the night-time checking is a sign it’s grabbed hold. NHS Talking Therapies help with exactly this kind of worry, and you can refer yourself. Would you consider that?
SCA_MODELS.why: Names health anxiety respectfully and offers support she can choose

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe. If it stops me checking my neck all night, yes.

For the reflux: smaller evening meals, not eating late, and I’ll prescribe a four-week trial of an acid-reducing tablet. We’ll review in four weeks, and if the feeling hasn’t settled, I’ll refer you to the ear, nose and throat team to take a look.
SCA_MODELS.why: Concrete plan with a defined review and escalation

SCA_MODELS.text: And here is exactly when to contact me sooner: if food or drink starts sticking, if swallowing hurts, if your voice becomes hoarse for more than a few weeks, if you feel a lump in your neck, if you lose weight without trying, or if it becomes one-sided. Those would mean an urgent referral, and I’d arrange it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Precise safety-net listing the red flags that would trigger referral

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That actually helps, knowing what to look for instead of just worrying.
Can you tell me in your own words why I think this is globus?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back on the reasoning, not just the plan

SCA_MODELS.text: Because it gets better when I eat, and I haven’t got any of the warning signs. And the clearing and the worry keep it going.
Exactly. I’ll see you this week for the examination, and again in four weeks.

SCA_STEM.name: Asha Devi
SCA_STEM.recent: Reception note: “Worried about a lump in her throat for several weeks, asking for urgent tests. Very anxious.” No previous ENT or gastroenterology referral.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone consultation about a lump sensation in her throat.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG184 (GORD and dyspepsia in adults, 2014, updated 2019) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE CG123 (common mental health problems, 2011; withdrawn May 2024)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A midline lump sensation between meals, eased by eating, with throat-clearing and no true dysphagia or other red flags, is globus pharyngeus. Make a positive diagnosis, explain why it points away from cancer, treat contributors, and safety-net precisely.

points.t: A persistent feeling of a lump or tightness in the midline of the throat, present between meals and often eased by swallowing food or drink, with frequent throat-clearing. There is no food sticking, no pain on swallowing, no weight loss, no voice change and no neck lump. It is common and benign.

points.h: Eased by eating is the key discriminator
points.t: An obstructing lesion causes true dysphagia: food physically sticks, usually worse with solids and progressive. A sensation that improves when eating points away from obstruction.

points.h: Red flags that change the pathway
points.t: NICE NG12: dysphagia at any age → suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer (recommendations 1.2.1 and 1.2.7, amended 2025; this replaced urgent direct-access upper GI endoscopy). At 45 and over, persistent unexplained hoarseness or an unexplained neck lump → consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer; a persistent unexplained neck lump also meets the oral cancer criterion. Also ask about pain on swallowing, one-sided symptoms, ear pain, weight loss, smoking and alcohol.

Reflux: lifestyle measures and, if there are reflux symptoms, a trial of a proton pump inhibitor (NICE CG184; dose and duration per BNF). Reduce habitual throat-clearing (sipping water instead), which perpetuates the sensation. Treat post-nasal drip if present.

points.h: Health anxiety is part of the treatment
points.t: Name the anxiety without dismissing the symptom. Explain that undirected tests rarely settle health anxiety and can find incidental results. Offer NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) for persistent anxiety, in line with stepped care (NICE CG113 for anxiety disorders; CG123 was withdrawn in 2024).
Any red flag, symptoms that progress, or globus persisting despite treatment → ENT assessment (nasendoscopy). Reassurance is safe only once the red flags have been asked about explicitly.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Identity check; open question; lets her voice the fear and the request before asking focused questions.
Colleague’s diagnosis, night-time checking and searching, others noticing the throat-clearing, impact on sleep and work.
Links the start of symptoms to the colleague’s diagnosis; picks up the neck-checking as health anxiety.
Idea (throat cancer like her colleague); concern (cannot stop worrying); expectation (every test, a camera and a scan).
One face-to-face neck and throat examination; no undirected tests; ENT referral if persistent or any red flag.
Globus with reflux and throat-clearing versus oesophageal, laryngeal or pharyngeal cancer; tests the eased-by-eating feature.
Explicitly asks about dysphagia, odynophagia, hoarseness, neck lump, weight loss, lateral symptoms, ear pain, smoking and alcohol; knows the NICE NG12 routes.
Names globus as a positive diagnosis and explains the reasoning in her own terms.
Reflux measures and a PPI trial (NICE CG184, dose per BNF), reduced throat-clearing, NHS Talking Therapies offered; resists an anxiety-feeding battery of tests.
Addresses health anxiety and reassurance-seeking as part of treatment, not an afterthought.
Named red flags that trigger urgent referral; examination this week; review at 4 weeks with ENT if not settled.

social.t: A colleague’s or relative’s cancer diagnosis commonly triggers health anxiety and body-checking. Ask about timing and support at work.
Night-time searching, neck-checking and constant throat-clearing are part of the cycle. Name them gently and offer alternatives.

legal.t: Do not speculate about the colleague’s diagnosis or compare cases. Keep the discussion on the patient’s own features.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024) expects care based on clinical need. Declining undirected tests is defensible when red flags are explicitly excluded and documented, with a clear route to referral.
Record the red flags asked about and their absence, the diagnosis given, the safety-net advice and the review date.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) for health anxiety; community pharmacy advice on reflux measures.

redFlags: True dysphagia (food sticking) at any age: suspected cancer pathway upper GI endoscopy (NICE NG12)
Persistent unexplained hoarseness or an unexplained neck lump at 45 and over: consider head and neck suspected cancer pathway (NICE NG12)
Pain on swallowing, one-sided symptoms, ear pain, weight loss, smoking or heavy alcohol use
psychosocial: Onset linked to a colleague’s throat-cancer diagnosis
Constant throat-clearing that others have noticed
ice: Idea: “It’s throat cancer, like my colleague.”
Concern: cannot stop thinking about it; needs certainty
Expectation: referral for every test, a camera and a scan

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is globus: a real feeling of a lump in the throat when nothing is there. It gets better when you eat, which is the opposite of what a narrowing would do, and you have none of the warning signs.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of a smoke alarm that goes off when you make toast. The alarm is real, but there’s no fire. Reflux and throat-clearing are the toast, and worry turns up the alarm’s volume.”

management.reflectIce: “Since your colleague’s news, this has been on your mind day and night. I want you to leave with an explanation you believe, not just a list of tests.”
management.psychosocial: Name the checking cycle; offer NHS Talking Therapies as her choice; agree to reduce searching and neck-checking.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face neck and throat examination once
Reflux lifestyle measures and a 4-week PPI trial (NICE CG184, dose per BNF); sip water instead of throat-clearing
Review at 4 weeks; ENT referral if not settled
safetyNet: Food sticking, painful swallowing, hoarseness lasting weeks, a neck lump, weight loss or one-sided symptoms: contact for urgent referral

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Reassurance is a skill that this station marks directly. Candidates fail by giving it too early (without the red flags), too thinly (“it’s nothing”), or not at all (referring for everything).

items.fail: Reassuring before asking about food sticking, voice change, neck lump and weight loss.
items.why: Reassurance without red-flag exclusion is unsafe and scores poorly in Tasks.
items.fix: Ask the red flags explicitly and tell her you have: “Those are the warning signs, and you don’t have them.”

items.fail: Referring for endoscopy and a scan to end the consultation.
items.why: Undirected tests do not fit UK practice for classic globus and reinforce health anxiety.
items.fix: Explain why, offer one examination, and give clear referral triggers.

items.fail: Calling it globus but not explaining why.
items.why: An unexplained label does not reassure; examiners want reasoning shared with the patient.
items.fix: Use her own answer: “It eases when you eat; a narrowing would make eating worse.”

items.fail: Never linking the onset to the colleague’s diagnosis.
items.why: The trigger is the hidden agenda; missing it leaves the fear untouched.
items.fix: “Did this start before or after you heard about your colleague?”

items.why: Patients hear “all in your head”. The symptom is real and has treatable contributors.
items.fix: “The feeling is real; worry turns up its volume. We’ll treat both.”

items.fail: Safety-netting with “come back if it gets worse”.
items.why: Vague safety-netting is standard failing feedback, and here it undermines safe reassurance.
items.fix: Name the triggers: food sticking, painful swallowing, hoarseness, neck lump, weight loss, one-sided symptoms.
